utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Krajisnik, you provided us again with some documents. I think most of them untranslated. I did the same as I did before; I distributed them among the parties so that the parties can see to what extent they think it useful for the Chamber to introduce them into evidence. If, finally, nothing would be done, and if you have any very specific requests to say this document is for this reason very important, you can do that at the end of your testimony, after the parties have considered whether or not to tender them and to introduce them into evidence. Then I'd like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, and I would like to give an opportunity to you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, excuse me. Yesterday I took the two transcripts, the two records regarding Arkan's men. Those are the first two documents that related to Arkan's men that I would like to explain. They are not new. They are in evidence. And they have to do with Panorama, which I realised when I reviewed them. There is one document making a reference to Russian automatic weapons. Maybe they don't need to be in evidence but I would like to explain. It's all in OTP documentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, if you would like to say something more, because yesterday, almost at the end of your examination, the issue of Arkan's men residing in the Panorama Hotel was raised. If you would like to add anything to your testimony in this respect, please do so, because it appeared in two documents, both being reports, from what I remember, of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Here I have a record of a government -- a cabinet session, dated the 29th of July, 1992. The last numbers are 462. It's the last page of that record, speaking of Panorama. I will read. It's AB 25 -- or AD 25. If you don't have it, we can put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not -- I don't know whether it's quite clear to me what AB stands for, the numbering.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, it's an item in it. It's an item in the record. It's an item of the agenda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you tell us, if you have got it there, unless one of the parties would mind if Mr. Krajisnik reads a portion of the agenda of the -- of what I understand to be the cabinet meeting -- yes, cabinet session, 29th of July, and you tell us on the basis of what you know that one of the items on the agenda, number 25, would be what exactly, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has to do with the Panorama, and it could shed some light on affairs related to Arkan's men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you take it from a document, perhaps put that on the ELMO so we can see what is in the document, because I also do understand that you had no personal recollection of --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, based on the ERN, we have been able to locate the English translation. There are a number of ways of dealing with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think we can either send it -- it can either be put on the screen electronically, I think, or it can be sent to the registrar and be immediately printed and I leave it that to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps that's the best way of dealing with it. And I do see that one of the documents Mr. Krajisnik has, he put something in yellow. It should be in front of you. Let's have look at it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I marked it. I highlighted certain passages so you can see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please read slowly to us what it says under --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I then put it in front of me? Because you have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you can read it from your screen, it would be better for the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let Mr. Krajisnik have our copy and then the other one can be on the screen. That seems a good compromise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm told we can -- this can be sent to the Chamber so you can be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have the originals. The B/C/S, not the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's what I was referring to, that we could provide the English translation immediately, if that's useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you have sent it already to Mr. Registrar or not? Because what we then could do is to have, at 25, which takes only one-third of the page, together with the translation, have that on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It has been sent and Mr. Registrar is waiting for the receipt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. He's now printing it, and then Madam Usher, once we have the English translation, could you please add the English translation just above. So zoom out a little bit and have the English translation on top of -- yes. Paper tray is empty. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: While this is being done, do my learned friends know whether this has been exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Given the date, I'd say there is a strong probability, but we'll check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could already start if you just slowly read agenda item 25. We are aware that the interpreters are now translating just from this document, and of course that's different from having time and having a possibility to look up whatever one wants to look up. Could you please slowly read, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "It has been concluded that the costs of accommodation and food provided in facilities Panorama and Buducnost be paid for refugees and the wounded who are there for convalescence after hospital treatment. It has also been decided to take over facilities Panorama and Buducnost starting with the 1st of August as assets for defence requirements, to conclude contracts with them providing for payment of accommodation and catering with the proviso that an obligation be imposed on the refugees to contribute to the costs of accommodation and catering in an amount to be agreed. The costs of accommodation and food for the wounded would be paid in full."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is also a record of a Presidency session of the 3rd of July that is related to this document from which we can see that the Buducnost facility housed the wounded whereas the Panorama building was used for housing refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Just one additional question, Mr. Krajisnik, in this respect. You were staying in the Panorama Hotel. Who else of, well, let's say the persons whose names we have frequently heard, were there apart from you? Any other government officials or -- I don't remember, as a matter of fact, at this moment although it may have been said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. There was a large number of people there in addition to refugees from the Assembly, from the government, and there are only 30 to 40 double rooms there, whereas this is a reference here to 20 Arkan's men. They could have been in a different building. These two only shared the same management, and that's why I wanted you to see the record of that Presidency session, 3rd of July. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although, of course, the Presidency session doesn't say anything about government officials in Panorama.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So-called meeting -- no, no, no. Please, there are just two lines here, if you could read them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I -- let me just -- yes. The only thing I'm referring to is that apart from refugees and wounded, there is no further specification given. It doesn't say refugees, government officials, or government -- or refugees, paramilitaries, or refugees, soldiers. It doesn't say anything. But let's -- you've drawn our attention.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the wounded were in Buducnost building. It's written here. Whereas Panorama housed refugees. Somebody just lumped it together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But what I'm saying is that it does not mention in any way government officials, which, as I understand, were residing in Panorama as well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is this an exhibit at this moment or is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Not absolutely sure it was an exhibit. It was among all the hyperlinked material that we had in court during Mr. Krajisnik's evidence. We can check that. Mr. Sladojevic can look on his list.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The Court is referring to the Presidency session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm now referring to the government session of the 29th of July in which this agenda item 25 appears. And as a matter of fact, it seems that it is a -- yes, it's 29th of July. It seems to be the 43rd session of the government, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We have got a complete English translation. Was that the issue just now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, we have that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: With that ERN number. We've got a proper ET ERN document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have it in front of us. If the parties would please try to find out in silence whether it is exhibited. If it is, we would like to hear the number. If it's not, the parties could -- perhaps then it would be good that it would be -- become an exhibit because Mr. Krajisnik has testified about this document. Anything else at this moment, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I would just like you to see this other document showing that Buducnost housed the wounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any dispute? The report we saw yesterday was only about Panorama. Is there any -- is there any dispute that wounded people were housed in this other building, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: None that I'm aware of at this time, Your Honour. I would have no basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has no relevance for you at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that different for the Defence? No, same. So then we leave it to the Panorama at this moment, Mr. Krajisnik. Yes, Mr. Tieger you may proceed. Oh, yes, Judge Hanoteau has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krajisnik, you were staying at the Hotel Panorama. How many people stayed at the hotel at the same time as you? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 35 at the most. 45 rooms in two pavilions. They were double rooms and it was full. Full of refugees. I was a refugee myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if the president will allow me, I found one document showing that there existed Russian-made automatic weapons. It's an OTP document, if I may show it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you've -- do you mean Russian-made automatic weapons after the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no -- yes, yes. Automatic weapons, but from the period from 1949 to 1957. Those with the drum barrels that I tried to explain, which is completely different from later, modern automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes but -- no, Mr. Krajisnik. You were just interpreting, without any specific knowledge, just on the basis of the wording of what we found in this report, you were -- you were looking at whether any inferences could be made, you made some inferences, which I expressed some doubt as to whether there was an objective justification for these inferences. In that context, I asked myself, and to that extent of course you as well, whether Russian automatic weapons could be automatic weapons produced later. I don't think that this was excluded, and if we want to pursue that matter, we should do that thoroughly and systematically and I leave it at this moment to the parties to see whether we should give it any follow-up. Not as far as I'm concerned. Therefore --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't have any objective knowledge or information, you are right about that. I was just trying to give my interpretation, and thank you for allowing me that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Prosecutor Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to conclude our discussion or questions and answers about Arkan and Arkan's forces. Yesterday you described the extent of your familiarity with Arkan and Arkan's forces, and I'd like to ask you now, then, to turn to tab 149, where we find P1021.1A. That's a portion -- or a video footage from an interview of you in 1993, in May of 1993, I believe, and it's a document we've seen before. And as you will recall, I believe, there is a question from a viewer about Arkan's statement regarding acts of deputies, and your answer was: "I think that Mr. Arkan has many positive and significant credits when it comes to the Serbian people. So when I consider his negative statements, the balance is still positive." Mr. Krajisnik, what were the many positive and significant credits that Mr. Arkan had when it came to the Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about any positive contributions by Mr. Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when you stated to the individual viewer and to the television audience that you thought that he had many positive and significant credits, to what, then, were you referring?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after this, I inquired about the truth of the matter, and I now know what it was all about. I found the documents. At that time, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I'd like to invite Mr. Krajisnik to explain what the whole of the answer was about, but it's -- You said you inquired into the matter. I do understand that it has got something to do with deputies banned to come to the parliament. You say this is what did not happen. And it was about a statement by Mr. Arkan regarding acts of deputies of Republika Srpska at all Serbian Assembly and at the previous Assembly. Could you tell us which Assembly he was referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not about the Serb Assembly but the Serbian Assembly, the one in Belgrade. Mr. President, I'll explain. Right away. There was the Vance-Owen Plan on the agenda and late Mr. Milosevic organised an all-Serb Assembly, inviting all deputies from Montenegro, the Serb Krajina, Republika Srpska, and Serbia, and at this enlarged forum, he wanted to force us to accept the Vance-Owen Plan. We sent four men -- or rather, four people; Mr. Buha, Mr. Jovo Mijatovic, Mrs. Plavsic, and I don't know who the fourth person was. At that Assembly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'm going to stop you. Could you tell us when that Assembly was held, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a document, although not right here. I can show you. It was in 1993. January, maybe February, 1993. I don't know exactly but I have a document that I can show you. It was published.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It gives us a time frame, although not very precise. I don't know whether we need any more precision at this moment but at least it's early 1993. Thank you. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Arkan was an MP in the Serbian Assembly, and at this session, he stated that Mladic had banned the deputies of Republika Srpska to attend this Serb Assembly. And then there was this TV programme when I didn't want to increase the tensions with Serbia. Whereas Arkan, as an MP, defended certain interests and passed off certain stories as an MP, I said that he's a man who did some good things because I didn't want to increase tensions with Serbia. They were about to impose sanctions on us. Whereas Mladic had said that RS deputies were banned from attending that Assembly. That's why I said that he did something good, meaning he did it as an MP. And I wouldn't have said this -- I wouldn't be saying this now if I hadn't inquired into it thoroughly. I can show you all the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, we also discussed Seselj and Seselj's men yesterday. Now, his groups included those --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In that connection, Your Honour, if we could distribute the next item.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I produce that document about Arkan, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it to the parties whether there is any --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I meant it only if it's needed. If it's not needed, fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for offering it to us, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I or should I not? I didn't quite understand. It is from the Politika daily newspaper, has articles and his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd encourage Mr. Krajisnik to hand the document to someone, because of course the parties can't explore the matter if they aren't given a copy of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you're invited to pass a copy of the document you had in mind to Mr. Registrar so that the parties can look at it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd do that tomorrow. I haven't got it here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, as I began to ask, it's correct that Arkan -- excuse me, that Seselj's groups included those led by Slavko Aleksic, Mirko Blagojevic - both of those found at page 1 in the English of the order and page 1 of your version as well - Branislav Gavrilovic, aka Brne, found on page 3, and Jovo Ostojic, among others?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, yes, we did meet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And indeed from time to time, Mr. Seselj himself met with members of the Bosnian Serb leadership, including yourself, during the period 1992 through, let's say the first half of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Once we found it here, that he visited Pale after these vojvodas were proclaimed. Now, was he with me? I believe he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe although I indicated that the document needed a number, I'm not sure we actually assigned one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We didn't do so, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1226, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And it's correct, isn't it, that Mr. Seselj supported the efforts of the Bosnian Serb leadership and the Bosnian Serbs because he understood from his meetings with the Bosnian Serb leadership that you were pursuing objectives that he also sought.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if his objectives were like ours, then all right. But there is a certain degree of differentiation here. What do you consider his objectives to be? He supported us in every period of crisis when the official authorities from Serbia attacked us. That's when we needed support.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we can look at tab 153.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Which will need a number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1227, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Which reflects in part the comments of Mr. Seselj in June, 1993, the month following his meeting with you and Dr. Karadzic after the vojvoda ceremony. And if we can turn to page 3 of the English and, Mr. Krajisnik, to 02088799, the very bottom of the first column and the top two paragraphs of the middle column, Dr. Seselj is saying, speaking about a Serbian state, which could be called, for example, Western Serbia, and stating: "That would finally resolve Serbian national issue or better said, that would signify the realisation of the national interests and goals of the current combat of Serbs western from Drina River. Western Serbia must be --"

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I took the other one but I haven't got it here. I'm sorry. I hope it's not a problem for you. It's very hard to see this because of the binding. "Ovations for Duke Seselj"? Is that what you're reading from? This is the first time I see this, so I would like to read it. If the subheading is "Ovations for Duke Seselj," then that should be it. Is that what I'm supposed to read?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, it's under that portion, correct. And the portion I was just reading from begins a little more than halfway through the second paragraph, and as I say, it's found at the very bottom of the far left-hand column, Mr. Krajisnik. And then we'll continue on to the middle column.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "Western Serbia," Mr. Seselj stated, "must be equal federal unit and in order to realise that as soon as possible, it is necessary to completely liberate and mark Serbian territories in Republika Srpska. The only thing left to do would be to take (liberate) Orasje, Srebrenica, Gorazde and some parts of Serbian Herzegovina and Serbian Sarajevo, and that job would be done." He goes on to say that: "Then Muslims wouldn't have any option but to accept the division ..." and then he continues on the next paragraph, referring to his support for the SDS, including: "Serbian Radical Party is again honouring Serbian Democratic Party, said Seselj, and we shall never forget or deny the fact that SDS was the first one to rise for the Defence of Serbian national interest and its dignity. They organised and spiritually enlightened Serbian people and started the combat for the creation of Serbian state on the territory of former Bosnia and Herzegovina." And he goes on, and I'll certainly read -- invite you to read that paragraph. He goes on to talk about the war and the Vance-Owen Plan and maps.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. That's -- those remarks are a reflection of Mr. Seselj's understanding of the uniformity of view on a number of important issues and regarding events in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Republika Srpska between him and the Bosnian Serb leadership.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, this is a programme of the Serb Radical Party that he presented here in court as well. And the -- and the Presiding Judge, Judge Orie, is going to try Mr. Seselj in this Court. This is what Mr. Seselj is saying, but he was not in charge of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The responsibility was that of the Serb Democratic Party. So if it were the other way around, if the SDS supported what he was saying, then that would be different, but this is, in his view, supportive of the good things, as he believes, of the SDS -- things that the SDS did. We didn't ask anyone to do anything, so it's not an identical programme. These are two different parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik -- excuse me -- during the course of your examination-in-chief, you had occasion to comment on the issue of the shelling of Sarajevo, and in particular, on May 14th -- or May 24th, excuse me, in connection with testimony during the Prosecution case on the shelling of Sarajevo, you said, at page 88, line 2: "As for any other assessments in terms of whether something like that happened or not, nor do I know. There was this accusation all the time about Sarajevo being shelled and there were exchanges of gun-fire, but I really cannot remember anything special." Now, another Prosecution witness, General Wilson, testified that Sarajevo suffered a horrific bombardment on the 14th of May, 1992, when something on the order of 5.000 to 10.000 rounds were fired into the city, and he described it as extensive, indiscriminate, and disproportionate. And in connection with the 14th of May, 1992, I'd ask you to turn now to tab 55, and I don't know if those binders have been distributed yet.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 24th of May or the 14th of May?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Those materials will need to be distributed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, in English, we find on the transcript, and that's what I remember Mr. Tieger said, is the 14th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But before that, he said the 24th of May, so I was wondering whether he accidentally made a mistake. I heard the interpretation, and it said the 24th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's why I'm clarifying the matter. On the transcript it appears in English that he said twice the 14th of May, but that's at least what he meant to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the confusion may be that when I referred to Mr. Krajisnik's testimony during the examination-in-chief, that was the 24th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But the shelling in Sarajevo to which I'm referring, and the date is the 14th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It was the 24th of May, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Is there an index with this presentation?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe there will be. I don't know if you have the materials yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Tab 155 arrives but at this moment without an index. I take it that you'll soon find it, Mr. Tieger, so let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, this is an intercepted telephone conversation between Mrs. Plavsic and Radmila on the 14th of May, 1992. The best information I have at this point, unfortunately, is that it is in evidence but as P64A, and obviously it needs more specific identification and we'll provide that for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, as you can see from the transcript of this conversation, Mrs. Plavsic is speaking to Radmila, and when Radmila asks her, "How are you?" Mrs. Plavsic says, "Listen." And then Mrs. Plavsic says: "Can you do anything, do you know how this building is being shelled?" And then she describes it as a horror. A little further down: "It's a horror, are they thinking ... let me tell you, it's a disaster." And then on the second page of the English, and the second page of your version as well, Mr. Krajisnik, Mrs. Plavsic states: "Tell me, please, do they really have to shell civilian targets?" And Radmila says: "I must not tell you anything, I was told not to disclose any information over the phone ... we can't ..." Mrs. Plavsic says: "Yes, yes. All right, all right." Radmila: ... give today. The situation is such that one cannot say anything about it, you know." And further on, toward the end of the conversation, the brief conversation, Mrs. Plavsic says: "... only, I was wondering if civilian targets must really ..." And Radmila says: "What is being done, had to be done, that is all I can tell you." Now, this conversation, Mr. Krajisnik, occurred at a time when Mrs. Plavsic, as you indicated previously, was still in Sarajevo, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, she was in Sarajevo, yes. The 20th of May, the 22nd, the 24th, until when was she in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court, please, who Radmila was?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that that's a secretary in the MUP. I know that there was some Radmila who was a secretary in the MUP in Braca.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that's the RS MUP, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. If that's the person it is. There was this Radmila in the Serb SUP -- MUP in Braca at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So as -- it's correct that Mrs. Plavsic was aware and Radmila was also aware of the shelling that took place on the date testified to by General Wilson.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, but I can remind you that on the 13th of May, Mladic talked to Unkovic and he said we have to observe the cease-fire, remember? It was on our agenda yesterday. There was some reason here for this shelling. I don't know. Mladic said that to Unkovic only a day before. He was talking about Arkan's men. We have to observe the cease-fire, the one-sided cease-fire agreed upon in the Assembly. We had proclaimed a one-sided cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just one moment, Your Honour, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we turn next to tab 156, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe this will need a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 156 will be P1228, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I heard this audio tape too. I heard it here. You played it -- I know this conversation. From hearing it here, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, then, in that case we may double check about the number, Your Honour, but meanwhile in any event, Mr. Krajisnik, this is a telephone conversation between General Mladic and Mirko Vukasinovic on the 28th of May. And it begins with Mladic speaking and asking, "From where does your artillery shoot the best?" And continuing to inquire about where Vukasinovic suggested they shoot, talking about the number of salvos, where they should fire, and then, about halfway down through the conversation, General Mladic states: "Shoot at Velusici, and also at Pofalici, there is not much Serb population there ... shoot there, around Dobrovoljacka Street, up there around Humska ..." And they continue further, Mladic: "Understood?" Vukasinovic: "Yes, sir." Mladic: "And apply artillery reconnaissance, so that they cannot sleep, that we roll out their minds, drive them crazy." Vukasinovic: "Yes, sir." And then Mladic states: "Fire one more salvo at the Presidency." And Vukasinovic says: "Yes, General sir." Now, Mr. Krajisnik, isn't this another reflection of the extensive shelling of Muslim areas by Bosnian Serb forces in -- during this period of time, in roughly May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, there is a difference involved. You said the 14th of May and I focused on the 14th of May to explain what the situation was, and this is the 28th of May, when the barracks were dislocated. Remember? When the Muslims did not honour the agreement reached. But this is the first place where I heard this conversation. I don't know about the 28th of May. Well, if I'm supposed to explain, I can only relate this to when the column was cut in two, when they were dislocating the barracks, and I remember hearing the voice, but on the 18th of May, the agreement was reached and then on the 20th, the column was cut off and they did not honour the agreement. Maybe that was it. I don't know what the reason was. And I didn't know that this was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you were asked about the massive bombardment of Sarajevo during the course of your examination-in-chief and in response, you said that you really couldn't identify such a thing although there was talk about that. You were generally unfamiliar with that. Now, are you telling the Court that now there was massive bombardment of Sarajevo of which you were aware?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I'm afraid that either the interpreters are not interpreting my words properly or you're twisting my words. I remember exactly what I said. You asked me about one particular shelling that a protected witness here talked about. You asked me about a testimony. And I said that I do not remember what he said. I can't remember the exact date when this was. I really don't. There is this particular conclusion that states for political reasons do not shell or do not respond to gunfire. I did not know about the shelling that was referred to here, without a particular date that was -- without giving a particular reference, a date. Now, that's what I'm talking about. Now, are you asking me do I know whether Sarajevo was shelled? I heard about that. I mean, heard about it. I heard about it from foreigners who were telling me that Sarajevo was being shelled, and then the military was saying we are just responding in kind. And we said, for political reasons do not even respond because this is a hindrance to our conference, because we kept getting that answer all the time, that they are attacking us and that they are defending us. That is what our military told us when this was a hindrance in the conference. But you asked me only about one particular testimony, and that's the only answer I gave. So I will answer every question you may have, but let us know what we are talking about. And I don't like it when people are trying to catch each and every word that I say. We are serious people. I want to say the truth here. I'll tell you everything. I did not say what you said a few minutes ago. I said what I had to say about the testimony of a protected witness, and let me not mention the person's name because you know who this is, that was a witness who gave evidence about some kind of shelling that Mladic had conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'm just going to let your examination-in-chief stand. It's available to the parties, it's available to the Chamber, it's available to you on tape as well. But let me ask you this: You just heard an intercept with General Mladic saying apply artillery reconnaissance so that they cannot sleep. Drive them crazy. That's an intercept of May 28th, 1992. Before that date, were you aware from any source, including General Mladic, that it was his intention or inclination to engage in shelling of that manner?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And I said that when that witness testified. I said then I wasn't there and I didn't know, and I said it when the witness was here. When he said that allegedly Mr. Karadzic, Mrs. Plavsic, Mr. Koljevic, and I were there when Mladic said those words. I didn't know what he was talking about. I was president of the Assembly. What am I to do with him? I couldn't either order it or forbid it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Krajisnik be asked to speak at a more decent speed that lends itself to interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you're invited to speak at a lower speed because the interpreters have difficulties in following your velocity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't go to see my dentist, Your Honour. I forgot. They moved my appointment to Wednesday and I have toothache now and that's why I'm a bit temperamental, but I'll try to speak more slowly. And they asked that you give me permission to make it to that appointment, from 8 to 9 on Wednesday. That's what my doctors asked me to convey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will then consider that. That would be --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The week to come, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Mr. Krajisnik, subsequent to May 12th, were you aware that General Mladic or his forces were engaging in extensive, indiscriminate, and disproportionate shelling of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, whenever foreigners gave such reports, not to me but to others, to the effect that we were shelling Sarajevo, and whenever we asked the military, the military would always tell us that their infantry was trying to break out through our defence lines and they are responding with artillery. That was always the answer we got. Not I but others. But I mean I was there when they talked. It was senseless, otherwise, to spend so much ammunition and keep men engaged there if you didn't want to take Sarajevo, if that was not your intention. It would have been a waste. I was not responsible for it but I would never have agreed to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well my first question, of the two I just asked, Mr. Krajisnik, was about your awareness from any source, including General Mladic, that such shelling and bombardment might be part of his tactical repertoire. And in that connection, let me ask you to turn to the 16th session of the RS Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that. I know what he said in Knin. He spoke in Knin and people even applauded because they didn't know what that meant. They thought there would be no war in our parts. I heard him speak for three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, the first passage I want to bring your attention to is found at page 47 of the English and page 8 -- 00847750 of your version, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And it's found toward the bottom of the page, about a dozen lines from the bottom or so. And General Mladic states: "I do not want to fight the war like that, to lose men, we will go 400 metres in front of the tank so that the enemy cannot strike the tank with a Zolja or an Osa ... The tank shell has a range of 3 kilometres, a 100 millimetre gun of 3 kilometres, and his sniper can shoot at me from 600 metres. I will put the infantry forward 400 metres in front of the tank to protect the tanks, to protect the artillery. With artillery I will clear the path for the soldiers, what do I care, I do not have to go down volunteer street. I shell him until I have driven him crazy." And one more passage, Mr. Krajisnik, at page 40 of the English and the bottom of 7744 of your version in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "If we want to make the Muslims surrender, 300 guns must be densely planted around Sarajevo --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask, can you give us the reference for that line, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's very densely printed. I cannot find the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That will be starting at the very bottom.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I found that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And very top of the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I receive some B/C/S on the English channel. There must be --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And for the benefit of English speakers, it's found at the top portion of page 40, approximately 8 lines down. Seven or eight lines down. And again: "If we want to make the Muslims surrender, 300 guns must be densely planted around Sarajevo, of calibre ranging from Zolja 40 to 64 millimetres to Orkan and P65 rockets. And Sarajevo, I don't need any applause, mate. I am not doing it for that or for recognition, I am just doing it to avenge the bones of my dead comrades." And then he goes on to describe the actions he took in Zadar. Mr. Krajisnik, you chaired that session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly on May 12th, 1992, in Banja Luka and you heard General Mladic describe exactly what he proceeded to do. Isn't it therefore correct, Mr. Krajisnik, that General Mladic told the Bosnian Serb Assembly, the Bosnian Serb leadership gathered there, precisely what he intended and was true to his word?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Prosecutor, I didn't find the passage but if you read the line here when he says, "It's genocide; we cannot do that," that's the one I read. And I understood that he's not going to commit genocide. As for the technique of his warfare in Knin, I didn't realise he was going to wage that kind of war in our parts. Read this passage here where he criticised one deputy who said that Muslims should be driven out. And he spoke for three hours. I got tired of listening to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I think Mr. Tieger has drawn your attention not to what was supposed to have happened in Knin but what Mr. Mladic said about what he thought should be done for Sarajevo. So would you please -- although now I do understand the last portion of your answer, that you said you were tired of listening at him, does that mean that when he spoke about Sarajevo, that you didn't listen because you were tired at that moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I mean, Mr. President, there was this long contribution by Mr. Mladic that got me tired, and my attention was flagging. I don't mean to say that I'm not interested in Sarajevo. I heard a lot of things, good ones and bad ones, but I didn't think he would -- it sounded more like propaganda, it sounded like he was speaking for the benefit of the media. That's what I was trying to say. He said about -- he said what he had done over there and that he would take some equipment and use it around Sarajevo, but eventually he didn't do it. And I remember the passage when he said this is genocide and we cannot do it that way. I remember that. And I remember the passage that concerns Sarajevo, but I understood it all as his propaganda because we were supposed to give him his appointment at that time. I didn't think of it as his plan. He says, I don't need your applause, I want to avenge my fallen comrades. That's what he said. Of course, if we could act with hindsight ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau was a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krajisnik, in this document we see that General Mladic says, and he's talking about the prisoners: "We will capture him and let us not play the game of taking prisoners and so on." [Interpretation] What he's saying all this in a very determined way, and I presume that this must be quite heavy to hear, yes? Do you think that you could intervene, as president of the Assembly? So I would like to ask you the following question: When you are chairing an Assembly session, could you say that you were against such thing? Could you go as far as interrupting? And could you say that such and such things were not bearable, for instance? Did you think that you could play this role?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, certainly, I could, but as far as I remember - because I didn't read this - he spoke about mercenaries that, according to Geneva Conventions, maybe killed. At least, in his interpretation. I don't know where it is written, but I don't think he was talking about Muslim prisoners. I would like to see that passage. I think -- I mean, I'm sure that he was talking about mercenaries. Under Geneva Conventions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please take the text that was read by the Prosecutor. It is the line that follows this text.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't find it. I didn't find that passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [In English] "I shell him until I have driven him crazy. Once we have driven him crazy he will either flee of his own accord, or, he doesn't even have to run away. Once we have approached we will capture him, and let us not play the game of taking prisoners."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's a different page. That's why I couldn't speak about it. Sorry, let me just try to find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, maybe you could give us the number of the B/C/S page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I should have done that. It's 00847750, and perhaps I can find the -- and it would be toward the very bottom of that page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had 44. He told me 44. That's where I looked for it. Yes. See here, he says: "Well done. Where is he? Do you want me to send him over to you? Keep him there. What do I want him for?" I remember well that he was talking about mercenaries from abroad even though I was speaking from memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me but I did ask you a question which was as follows: When you hear these kind of statements, and these statements were quite heavy, and these statements are not the type of statements that can reconcile people, I did ask you whether, as chairman of the Assembly, you thought that you could be the person who could intervene or could interrupt the session. Could you say that maybe people could have -- could talk differently in order not to poison the situation? I'm just asking you whether you thought, at the time, that it was possible, whether they are talking about mercenaries or Canadian, the fact is that they were talking about killing prisoners, so this is quite heavy. I don't know how you went through this but you were the president of the Assembly. Could you have intervened and said, "Please, I do not want to hear such things, could you please talk in a different way"? Could you do it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, I couldn't do anything. I could just not agree. I heard hundreds of heavier, worse things at Assembly sessions because people seem to think that a democracy is being allowed to tell whatever you please. It was such an atmosphere, and what mattered really were conclusions. In times of war you cannot tell a person, What are you talking about? Because he thinks it's his right. He managed to convince me here - and I remember his speech - that he had a right under the Geneva Conventions to kill a mercenary. I personally would never approve of that. I would never allow him to kill a man. But I remember the justification that he gave. But I neither agreed nor was I able to forbid anything. We could just talk at that Assembly and go our separate ways. All I could do was chair that Assembly and try to come to a high quality outcome, because, you see, people had lost family members - somebody lost a brother, somebody a mother - they were just venting. They were talking all sorts of things. And whenever you try to say anything in favour of the Muslims, they would accuse you of defending them. What really mattered for me was to arrive at good conclusions. I couldn't prevent anybody from doing anything. It's not that I didn't want to. I was trying to lead a wartime parliament that sometimes sounded as being full of warmongers. All I could say to him was, "What are you talking about?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one additional question to Mr. Krajisnik. You earlier said it was language used by Mr. Mladic because he didn't need applause, he needed to be appointed. So this is the kind of language you considered to be promotional for being appointed? Is that how I have to understand it, that this is the type of language you would consider to be supporting a future appointment by Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he was not seeking appointment, he was already appointed. But it was only propaganda. He was trying to come across as a great military leader, and that's what his reputation was. That's what he was trying to do. But he was also saying some good things here, like that he went to his village and managed to reconcile Muslims and Serbs. He said there should be no killing, there should be no expulsions. He said good things and bad things. It's a very long speech. You can read it. There are a lot of things lumped together.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Mr. Krajisnik said one thing at the end of his previous answer that we did not manage to pronounce - he speaks very fast - and that is Mr. Mladic was a legend, and if I had said something to him he could have responded with a "What the hell do you know?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Could we turn next to tab 157, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This will need a number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1229, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this will have to be read aloud; I see there is no translation. I should also indicate to the Court in connection with the newspaper articles of yesterday from December, 1991, and January, 1992, that the translations promised have been provided to the Court and we will endeavour to do precisely the same -- or that we have them here for distribution and will endeavour to do the same with respect to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, P1229 is an outgoing cable from UNPROFOR in Belgrade dated 30 May, 1992, and it is a summary of a meeting with President Milosevic held on 30 May, 1992, at 1200 hours. And I'll summarise it quickly for you and then read out slowly any -- any particular passages to which I want to bring your attention. First paragraph indicates that the meeting was requested by UNPROFOR to convey to President Milosevic the Secretary-General's message and that Morillon, MacKenzie and Auger were there on behalf of UNPROFOR. In the second paragraph, it reflects General Morillon's advisement to President Milosevic about the Secretary-General's action in response to the appeal of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the request to President Milosevic to use his influence with General Mladic to stop the bombardment of Sarajevo. President Milosevic expressed his complete disagreement with General Mladic's action, indicated that they had done their utmost to persuade him to stop the bombardment, and then it states: "While he could understand fighting in self-defence, there was no justification for the continued bombardment of the civilian population of Sarajevo. This was moreover not in the interest of Yugoslavia nor of the Bosnian Serbs." President -- and then the third paragraph, and it's the last one I'll turn your attention to: "President Milosevic indicated also that he had been trying to contact Mr. Karadzic to see if he could use his influence to stop the 'bloody, criminal' bombardment." And that is "bloody, criminal" bombardment. "He had so far not been able to do so. At our request, he promised to inform us of the outcome of his conversation with Karadzic when he is able to contact him." Mr. Krajisnik, this is a reflection, is it not, of the fact that the bombardment of Sarajevo was continuing through May and was known not only to those in Sarajevo but indeed outside the borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In my submission, Mr. Krajisnik needs to read the whole of this document. I've had a chance to scan it; it needs to be read in context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at the clock. Would it be a good idea if we would give an opportunity for Mr. Krajisnik to do that during the break? Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is in English. I can't read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. I'm told we can secure a B/C/S version in short order so that Mr. Krajisnik can have it at the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we then can have this printed out, if it's -- as I do understand, it's sent to Mr. Registrar, then we'll give Mr. Krajisnik the opportunity to read it in the original.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't know anything about this report or this bombardment. I could only interpret it not much better than you could. I don't know what I could possibly say in comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, Defence counsel of the accused has asked that you as a witness could have a look at this document as a whole and therefore questions will be put to you by Mr. Tieger, and the Chamber is following the suggestion of Defence counsel. So therefore, you as a witness get an opportunity to read this document in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, one other observation: We are firmly of the view that Mr. Krajisnik also needs a good break. It is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's a subject we may return to, in fact, after the break, but we make that observation strongly at this juncture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You did not know how long a break I had in mind, Mr. Josse. I was intending to extend it for three minutes so that Mr. Krajisnik would have both his break and time to read. Therefore, Mr. Registrar, if you could give the B/C/S document to Madam Usher, and so that the B/C/S version is given to Mr. Krajisnik so that he can read it, and we'll have a break until 20 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I was informed that you wanted to address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll make this brief, Your Honour. Could I first of all emphasise the matter I'm about to raise has not been discussed with Mr. Krajisnik at all. It's this: The Defence team contemplated what I'm about to say overnight. We were concerned yesterday about our client's general condition, demeanour, his ability to concentrate, and quite frankly, the quality of his answers. We decided as a team to see how he got on during the course of the first session today. In our submission, the situation has not improved. If anything, it's got worse. We had no idea about the toothache that he mentioned during the course of his evidence earlier. We note the comments on at least two occasions from the interpreters about the speed of his answers. He has been unable to find the place that he's been taken to, generally, with great care by my learned friend, with regularity; i.e., unable to find the place with regularity. Again, the general quality of his answers give rise to real concern. To state the obvious, Your Honour, the ordeal of being in the witness box for many consecutive days, save weekends and two bank holidays is physically exhausting and draining. That is compounded, in our submission, manyfold when the witness is the accused and that accused faces charges such as those that Mr. Krajisnik faces in this courtroom. The matter is further compounded by the hours of after-court work that Mr. Krajisnik clearly does in relation to his own case and his testimony. The Defence ask, in effect, for the Trial Chamber to weigh these various factors up and not sit tomorrow. As I say, Your Honour, I kept these submissions short. Mr. Krajisnik is not aware that I was going to say these particular matters, but we do have genuine concerns about the matter, and putting it colloquially, we submit that he really is flagging, and it's not surprising bearing in mind the ordeal that he's going through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before I give an opportunity for the Defence -- for the Prosecution to make whatever observations they would like to make, first I'm addressing you, Mr. Krajisnik. You've heard that Mr. Josse said that they -- the Defence team got the impression that your condition was such that we should not sit tomorrow and there was a general concern expressed about your condition, both physically and mentally. I would first like to know from you yourself, since of course there was no opportunity to discuss this with you, whether you consider your own condition such that a break in your testimony, at least for the day asked for, I'm not -- because that's the only thing at this moment Mr. Josse asked for, whether you would consider this to be a measure the Court should take. And just to tell you what approximately the criterion would be is that this Chamber wants to proceed, but if there -- if it would be inappropriate to proceed tomorrow because of your condition, we have to consider not to proceed tomorrow. But therefore it's not a question of whether it's more convenient or whether it is -- because the Chamber fully understands that testifying for so many days in your own case is certainly asking a lot from you. To some extent, of course, this is the consequence of your choice to testify in your own case, but that would be approximately where we have to strike a balance, but I would first like to know whether, first of all, whether you have any observations to make in respect of your own condition at this moment, that is physically and mentally; and second, whether what consequences your observations in relation to your condition, in your view, should have, as far as sitting tomorrow is concerned. Could you please try to answer this rather long question, or these two questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am struggling for freedom here, and for my honour. I'm not even interested in my health or in my life. I'm interested in my honour and freedom. I'm annoyed when somebody does not believe something that I am saying as the truth, and probably my Defence saw that. I'm making an effort and I'm asking to be able to explain so that I could convince the Trial Chamber and others, and if I'm not allowed to do that, then I'm going to be upset any other day too. I swore to you and to God almighty that I would tell the truth. So that's the point. Fatigue has taken its toll, yes. Perhaps I could focus had I not testified for so long, but when something remains unfinished, and when something can be interpreted against me and I know that is not correct, that upsets me and angers me terribly. That's what I said. What I am like, all of you can see that better than me because people are partial, aren't they? And, of course, when I work late every night in order to gather all this material, then that does have certain effects. But I want the trial to be over as soon as possible. Of course, I don't want to meddle with these professional duties because lawyers and you see this much better. If a break is necessary, then all right. But the effect is that when I cannot show this thing about Russian automatic weapons and Arkan's men and whatever, then I get really upset because I feel that there is something hanging in the air and I know it's not correct. And I cannot correct all of that at the end of my testimony. Then I'd need five days. I am not guilty and that is why I'm struggling. So it is up to you and the Prosecutor to decide what you feel is best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you have not pointed at specific physical difficulties you are at this moment experiencing. You explained to us what makes you upset now and then during your testimony. One very specific question: Earlier today you were talking about your toothache. Would that, because it's the only specific complaint about physical not feeling well, would that cause you to ask for a further delay? I'm just now concentrating on this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll have a toothache tomorrow and the day after tomorrow, all the way up to Wednesday, Your Honour. On Wednesday I go to see the dentist. I want to be set free as soon as possible, and when I'm free, then I can see the dentist any time I like. Here I have to wait for a fortnight before I can see a dentist, for instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You share that fate sometimes with some other people in the Netherlands, as I'm aware of. But my question, listening to your answer, I do not understand your answer to be that the toothache is such that you would prefer for that reason not to sit until you have consulted the dentist. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The toothache will be there Monday, Tuesday, then that would mean that I shouldn't work on Monday or Tuesday. I know that I have this medicine inside and until that is removed and the crown placed, I know that I'm going to have a tooth problem. Perhaps it also results in some psychological problems, as my lawyers can see. I cannot see that because I'm partial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you inform us about the medicine you get for your toothache. If you want to do it in private session, of course, then --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. This was treatment of the nerve. The nerve was extracted and then this medicine was put in, and now that should be taken out and a crown placed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know what the medicine is? Do you know a name or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Your Honour. The nerve is no longer there. It was opened, this canal, and then they put this medicine in, and I don't know what this medicine is, and then they treat it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll understand the reason why I'm asking, Mr. Krajisnik, is because the Chamber wants to be satisfied that this medication does not influence your ability to testify, but since you do not know exactly what this medicine is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, does the Prosecution want to make any observations in relation to what Mr. Josse said and what Mr. Krajisnik told us?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, of course, Your Honour, the Prosecution is not in a particular position to make an assessment of Mr. Krajisnik's physical or mental condition that would be of particular utility to the Court beyond what the Court has been trying to seek from Mr. Krajisnik and perhaps beyond the observations of his counsel who have worked with him before. The Prosecution just wants to make sure that it's -- that we are clear on what the issue is and what the answers are. Mr. Josse seemed to raise the issue of Mr. Krajisnik's fitness to proceed based on his observations. I know the Court tried to inquire of Mr. Krajisnik to get as much of a definitive response as possible. I understood Mr. Krajisnik's response to be in large part used as an opportunity to express views related to other things. He did make some allusions to fatigue or his condition or to deferring to the judgement of his Defence counsel, so I just want to make sure that the Court is clear on whether Mr. Krajisnik's view is that he's in a suitable condition to proceed or not. I don't want to see a situation where he's in a position to later say, well, I thought I mentioned that my -- that I was tired or that I'm -- and in the course of a longer answer that wasn't directed solely to that issue. So that's my only observation at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krajisnik, you've heard what Mr. Josse said. You were given an opportunity to make your own observations. You've now heard what Mr. Tieger said. Is there anything you would like to add at this moment to what has been said so that the Chamber can take that into consideration when it will consider the matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't wish to say anything. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I see you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour. I, with respect, appreciate entirely the inquiry that has come from the Bench in relation to Mr. Krajisnik's physical condition and the medication that he is taking. And that's a proper inquiry to make and one that we fully support. However, the thrust of my submission was more in relation to general demeanour and, to use Mr. Krajisnik's word, fatigue. And Mr. Krajisnik said, "Fatigue has taken its toll, yes. Perhaps I could focus had I not testified for so long." And that is the primary point that we on his behalf were making in the submission earlier. And that's our primary point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. The Chamber will consider the matter and most likely we'll come back to it after the next break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First, Mr. Krajisnik, did you have an opportunity to review the document that was referred to shortly before we took the break?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, as I indicated in my earlier question, that document reflects that the ongoing bombardment of Sarajevo was known to many people and even those outside not only Sarajevo but the borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina. First of all, did you -- well, let me ask you more directly: Were you not aware of this ongoing bombardment of Sarajevo at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Today I said when the shelling took place I didn't know that there was shelling on the 28th of May, and when the witness was here I did not know that that was the date that the witness was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that there was just one date on which Sarajevo was shelled?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you about this shelling, the one that you're talking about, the 28th of May. Today, I found out that on the 28th of May there was shelling. We discussed shelling at a later session. We talked about shelling. And the first session of the Presidency was after the 12th of May, it was on the 31st of May. You saw that, a consultive meeting. And then on the 2nd or 3rd of June we discussed shelling and there is some conclusion about that. Mladic attended that meeting as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We'll get to that, Mr. Krajisnik. You said two things, in particular, during the course of your examination-in-chief. You said on the 23rd of May, at approximately page 69: "I can't identify any major shelling, particularly not with regard to Sarajevo's division." And you also said on the 24th of May, as I indicated earlier, in responding to testimony about the shelling of Sarajevo: "... whether something like that happened or not, nor do I know. There was this accusation all the time about Sarajevo being shelled and there were exchanges of gun-fire, but really I cannot remember anything special."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's exactly what I said and that's exactly what I think. When there was this discussion at the consultative meeting, it wasn't about any kind of large-scale shelling. It had to do with the complaints of the international community, and Mr. Koljevic talked about this and we wanted to have observers next to every one of our artillery pieces. You can find that in all the records of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you to look at the next exhibit and see if that constitutes something special. That would be found at tab 159.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: These are two video clips, Your Honour, with the accompanying transcript. And the dates can be seen on the transcript; June 7th and June 9th. Perhaps -- Your Honour, the transcript and the video clip will need numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first one, Your Honours, dated 7 June, 1992, would be P1230A; and the other one, dated 9 June, 1992, will be P1230B.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, whenever the Court is ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Then if we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will need to start again, I think. I don't know what you're receiving. I can see it on this monitor but not on the -- now I see it. If we could begin once more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "It was the symbol of modern Sarajevo. Now of its destruction. Flames tear across the floors and up into the highest storeys, showering debris onto the streets at the heart of the Bosnian capital. The disintegration of one of the city's UNIS towers reflected in the broken windows of its twin. "300 metres on, across the road, the parliament of this newly independent state is also struck. "It doesn't burn but the nearby Marshal Tito barracks do. Since its evacuation two days earlier, it's being systematically destroyed. Every night in Sarajevo you think it can't get worse, but it does, making a mockery of attempts of mediators to bring peace to this city which is enfolded in war. Less than 24 hours earlier, the Serb commanders had put their signatures on yet another agreement affirming a truce never adhered to, and their readiness to reopen the airport. Now, the Serb gunners in the hills show where their true commitment lies. Under a sickle moon, the city rocks to the explosions, lit up by fire and the mass of glowing sparks that drift across its roofs."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Next will be P1230B.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "Sarajevo is burning, in its heart and in its suburbs. "Suddenly on Sunday night the whole city becoming the target, no district spared. All shaking as every ten seconds the rocket shells and mortars land. The fire so heavy, so incessant that the deadly streams of light criss-cross each other."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you said you couldn't recall anything special with regard to shelling that occurred. Was what we just saw such a regular event that it no longer struck you as special?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not following this shelling of Sarajevo at all, this one of the 7th and the other one of the 28th. Through Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Koljevic, I heard that there were complaints that Sarajevo was being shelled. That's what foreigners told them. And there are sessions of the Presidency that show what we concluded. That is what I know. Pale, where I was, is 30 kilometres away from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So the action taken --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Judge Hanoteau has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, sir. You've use the worked "foreigners" twice. What does that mean exactly in your mind? You used this same word twice today, this afternoon. What do you mean by that? What does "foreigner" mean when you use that word?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, representatives of the UNPROFOR, General MacKenzie. MacKenzie met with Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When did you first hear complaints by foreigners about the shelling of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any complaints that I received myself, but I got news from Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Koljevic and Mrs. Plavsic, news of such meetings. I believe I attended one meeting with General Morillon, with Mrs. Plavsic, but we discussed other topics, such as humanitarian organisations, but I never met with General MacKenzie. I never talked to him. I know that we sought a UN observer to stand next to every soldier of ours because our military were telling us that we were only returning fire and we demanded from the UN that they place their observers. It's somewhere on record. I remember reading it. Because we were convinced that what the military were telling us was the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you referred to action taken by the Presidency. If you turn to tab 160, please. It's a document that has been seen before. These are the minutes of the 4th Expanded Meeting of the War Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 9th of June, 1992. Present at that session are Dr. Karadzic, Dr. Plavsic, Dr. Koljevic, yourself, Mr. Djeric, and General Mladic, Gvero and Tolimir are also there. After a briefing by General Mladic in detail about the overall situation, and a briefing by General Gvero on the situation in the area of the Banja Luka Corps, the Presidency concluded a number of things, including that the heavy artillery fire on the town be halted. Now, that's a decision by the Presidency to cease the bombardment of Sarajevo on that date; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Correct. There are items here and I can explain all of them. Well, that's exactly what I wanted to explain, and I can go through this item by item to tell you what transpired. This is the record that I had referred to earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, at the moment, Mr. Krajisnik, as you can see, I'm not asking you to go through item by item. I'm focusing on the third conclusion, that the heavy artillery fire on the town be halted.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. Because the military said, as it's written up here, that there is command out of control, or uncontrolled command, and all this is geared at putting all command under control and stopping the shelling of the city. And they were telling us, We were just returning fire. That's what the entire discussion was about. And you will see that if you read this record, that everything focused on this point, the four barracks, et cetera. This is the record of the Presidency session that I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Before that time, Mr. Krajisnik, had you or any other of those present, other than General Mladic and General Gvero and Colonel Tolimir, made any effort to determine the extent of the bombardment and the extent of the ordnance that was being dropped on Sarajevo, from the May 14th bombardment that Mrs. Plavsic complained about to Radmila, all the way through to the continuing bombardment referred to by Mr. Milosevic, and the bombardment that we saw on the video?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were people in charge of cooperation with the UNPROFOR, as far as I remember. Primarily it was Mr. Koljevic who contacted with Mr. MacKenzie. Mrs. Plavsic handled one part of the coordination concerning humanitarian affairs. Not all of us were in contact with the UNPROFOR.
