And what probably happened was that a complaint was received and, when the military representatives came, we had a discussion and they gave their reasons why that was being done. I don't remember anything about intensity or exact amounts, but I remember that this discussion was initiated by complaints made to our side by foreigners. And if these conclusions had not been adopted, I'm sure I would have rebelled against this, because if any shelling is being done, that's a crime, and it's not only that it's a crime, it's that it's politically damaging, as Mr. Milosevic said, for both sides, independently of the crime that is being committed. And there is another record where it said that observers should be brought in to control it, to act as verifiers, and we agreed to all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thereafter, Mr. Krajisnik, that is after the 9th of June, the bombardment was resumed, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm telling you, if it's on record, then of course complaints must have been made. Bring the record here. Of course, there must have been complaints through the usual channels, and we adopted the same conclusions. I know that we made a request for UN observers to be placed next to every artillery piece because our military was constantly telling us that they are only responding to fire from Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can find that record. I don't know which one that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Turn, please, to tab 161.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a statement by the Secretary-General to the Security Council on 26 June, 1992, Your Honours. It will need a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1231, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, as indicated, this is a statement to the Security Council by the Secretary-General on the 26th of June, 1992, stating: "I regret to inform the Council that the situation in Sarajevo has deteriorated considerably today. The Bosnian Serb forces have increased their bombardment of the area of Dobrinja, a suburb of Sarajevo close to the airport. UNPROFOR has reported that tank and infantry attacks were carried out and heavy artillery has been used against the civilian population. While the forces of the Presidency of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina have retaliated with attacks on two Serb-held areas, UNPROFOR has no doubt that the primary responsibility for the current bloodshed lies with the Serb forces, who are clearly pursuing their attempt to capture Dobrinja. This is occurring despite an agreement made public yesterday by the Serb side to stop shelling civilian areas and to abide by a unilateral cease-fire." First of all, Mr. Krajisnik, do you or do you not recall that bombardment in the latter part of June, 1992, in the area of Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the armed conflict around Dobrinja. Not shelling, though. I remember fighting around Dobrinja. I don't know if it was exactly on this date, but I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that fighting, in the area of Dobrinja, was an effort by Bosnian Serb forces to consolidate the areas that they already held into one portion, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Dobrinja is a settlement on the outskirts, an urban settlement, held by Muslims. There were Serbs there but consolidation was out of the question there, and it remained in Muslim hands after the war, with a very small piece held by Serbs. It was a suburb. It was just fighting in that suburb. I don't know who started it and I don't know who did what.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What do you mean "it was just fighting"? Just people fighting for reasons completely unknown to you, without any purpose, without any tactical objective?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that fighting went on throughout the war, in which one side would attack, the other side would defend itself, always on the line of separation, of demarcation. One thing is certain: Each time one side wanted to take control of one territory, the other side wanted to defend it. Of course everybody had their own different objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The Secretary-General's statement makes reference to a unilateral cease-fire, and you made reference earlier today to cease-fires.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Why was that cease-fire broken?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The best thing to do is to take this video and the statement of Mr. MacKenzie where he said that there were 19 cease-fires, all 19 of them broken by Muslims. We saw it here. I don't know who violated cease-fires, but we have his statement on tape. If there is anything else about it, tell me. I saw that video clip and I reviewed his statement in prison. There were 19 cease-fires, and all 19 were violated by the Muslims, according to him, and he was the Commander-in-Chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear or express any views about the purpose and use of cease-fires by Bosnian Serb representatives, either in the Assembly or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I don't rule it out. We always wanted cease-fires in order to continue negotiations. Of course, there were probably talks. If you have a specific example, let's discuss it. But let me not answer the question: We can hear what General MacKenzie said. We have the video clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, at the moment, Mr. Krajisnik, we are determining --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, Mr. Krajisnik is referring several times to a statement of General MacKenzie. I hope you'll forgive me but I don't have it just on the top of my mind what he's referring to. I take it that it is in evidence. Or is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't have a specific recollection at this moment either, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we please try to find out so that we can properly assess the importance of Mr. Krajisnik's testimony in this respect. Mr. Krajisnik, do you remember whether it was ever played here in this courtroom, the statement you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. That's why I gave you my DVD, and that statement of his is on that DVD. I first saw it when in prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If copies are made of the DVD, if there is any transcript of any statement of General MacKenzie, the Chamber would like to look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've got all the CDs, DVDs on my hard drive. If Mr. Krajisnik just makes it clear whether he's talking about today's or yesterday's, then that would help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it the last series you gave us this morning, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask, was it one of the five from yesterday, was it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it yesterday or don't you remember exactly when you gave it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think yesterday, certainly not today. I keep giving ever-new CDs, so I'm not sure. I think it was 11/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We will find it, Your Honour. If it's there, we'll find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, Mr. Krajisnik, I'd like to ask you, Mr. Tieger talked about, from what I understood, a unilateral cease-fire when he put a question to you, and said why was it violated? And then you said you should ask -- you should look at Mr. MacKenzie's cease-fire. That may well be. I take it that Mr. MacKenzie has referred to any cease-fire which was violated by the Muslims. That means that the Muslims committed, either unilaterally or through an agreement, to a cease-fire which then, as you said, Mr. MacKenzie said that they violated. But here if we are talking about a unilateral announced Serb cease-fire, then it needs an explanation why this unilateral cease-fire was violated. Do you know? If so, please tell us. If you don't know, please tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know but I can guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's stay out of guessing. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I had asked you whether or not you were aware of the Bosnian Serb view about cease-fires and how they might be used, and I think you said at that point, well, if there is such a statement, let's look at it. Let's turn, then, to -- back to the 16th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly on May 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could turn to page 22 of the English and 00847730 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You'll find the portion, Mr. Krajisnik - I'll wait until you get to the page - at the top half of the page, about ten lines down from the top. This is Dr. Kalinic speaking. After saying: "In other words, we must limit ourselves to what is militarily achievable. Also, I do not understand fully this statement, and I want it to be clarified here in this Assembly, what would the proclamation of a unilateral cease-fire mean for us. The reason stated was that by doing this, we would demonstrate to Europe that we are in favour of negotiations and a peaceful solution, but please, since we are in a closed session of the Assembly, let us make it clear: if we need a unilateral cease-fire to consolidate our armed forces and military forces, and I suspect that this may be the case, it should be made clear that this is just a statement for external public use. This statement may easily confuse our people, may inspire a certain degree of desertion, which would imply that we are slowly giving up on the warriors' military solution."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please. I read it. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That was an expression of the tactical use of an announced cease-fire for external political reasons which would allow Bosnian Serb forces, knowing that it was just used for that purpose, to consolidate. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, Mr. Prosecutor. I have to remind you of the statement of Mladic of the 13th of May when he said, in talking to Mr. Unkovic, we simply have to observe the cease-fire. Mr. Kalinic was saying this in resignation. He also said things like, We have to go to war, we have to win. I commented on this earlier. Find that conversation and you will see what Mladic meant when he talked to Unkovic on the 13th of May 1992. He said we have to observe unilateral cease-fires. It was just a day later. And that was our pure intention, to keep negotiating even while the war was going on. Negotiations were very important to us. Whatever people may have said here, negotiations were very important to us, and we didn't need any war to go on while we were negotiating. Although the matter of individual cease-fires is something different, I agree. Politically, the conference that was interrupted at this time on the 12th of May was necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you, in light of what you have just said about its importance, did you after Dr. Kalinic's remarks, say to the members of the Assembly, "No, Dr. Kalinic is wrong and don't be misled into thinking that the announcement of a cease-fire is for external purposes only. We really mean it and intend to abide by it," or words to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said, to esteemed Judge Hanoteau what the role of the speaker of the Assembly was. You know the example of that first session of the Assembly. People came with war on their minds from all sides to that first session. And if I had said to each of them what I could have said, like, you're wrong, you're wrong, you're wrong, you're wrong, I would have been speaker for 24 minutes only. Maybe I was pursuing tactical tactics. This man had family trapped in a basement. His wife was missing. Maybe he regretted it later, but that's what he said then, as an SDS party member, as an MP from the SDS. I didn't say anything, but of course I didn't think it justified. I didn't think it justified of anybody. I know it's incomprehensible to you because you live in peacetime, but this was war. In war it was very difficult to play arbitrator.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Please turn to page 49 of the English and page 37 of the B/C/S, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the number of the page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Not certain if Mr. Krajisnik said Mr. Kalinic was or was not an SDS member. Perhaps that could just be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you say that Mr. Kalinic was an SDS member or that he was not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He wasn't. He was from the Reformist Party, the reformist forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then there is a double mistake because the transcript now reads, "That's what he said then as an SDS party member, as an MP from the SDS," but I do understand that we have to understand this reference in our transcript as being a member of the Reformist Party. Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The page reference is 00 -- from the B/C/S, 00847752. It's in almost the precise middle of the page, Mr. Krajisnik. You are speaking, addressing the -- and summarising the discussion thus far. And you state - it's also in the middle of the page, at page 49 of the English: "A unilateral proclamation of a cease-fire, in political terms it is quite useful to have the Assembly of the Serbian people adopting, saying, there, we want to do it, see, we are letting the world see, we announce a cease-fire, we shall only defend ourselves, it's not our fault that the Serbs are always under attack, after all it is just an option." First of all, Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just be allowed to read what I said here? Only briefly. Because this is a summing up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Krajisnik, that is a reflection of or a response to or an acknowledgement of Mr. Kalinic's comments; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Look at the previous sentence when I said Mr. Kalinic is proposing military action, whereas we have to stick to politics. I know exactly what I said to him. I just read it. That is my answer to Mr. Kalinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, we will address the entirety of your remarks, but just above what this, the remark we just referred to, you say, "Although in my heart I believe that Mr. Kalinic is right, because we will surely go to war." And then, shortly afterwards, you raise again the issue of a cease-fire, and at that time, Mr. Krajisnik, you did not, did you, tell the political and military representatives of the Bosnian Serb people that Dr. Kalinic was dead wrong in proposing that cease-fires be used for cynical advantage and for external consumption?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said the opposite. And that's what is written here. And I'll explain it all. And everything I said is opposite to what you think. And I'll explain all of it. I did not support Kalinic. On the contrary, in a very nice way, I said that those who want to take other people's territories are in favour of a war option. That's what I said. Well, the fact that this is politics is a completely different matter, so if you take things out of context, you can give them a completely different meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Page 51 of the English, Mr. Krajisnik, page 38 of the B/C/S, page -- top of page 51.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it the same on the top of my page? Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: For you, Mr. Krajisnik, that would be the bottom -- the beginning of about the bottom quarter of the page at 00847753. Approximately a dozen lines from the bottom or so. "We are at war, and it will be possible to solve this thing with Muslims and Croats only by war."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That sounds like a war option, Mr. Krajisnik. Isn't that what you were saying?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. It does not sound like a war option. I am saying -- well, we are at war. There is a war on. And I'm saying that politics is going to be an instrument for bringing it to an end. War had already broken out. I am trying to summarise this by way of a conclusion that would be rational, and I succeeded in doing that. On the basis of all the belligerent statements made. This is not a conclusion. I am trying to keep people away from this war option and to say that politics will work this out. And that's the way it was. Read it to the end. Politics was an instrument for bringing this to an end. I don't know if I included all of it but I would like to ask you, before we bring all of this to an end, to adopt -- but I would like to ask you, before we bring this to an end, to adopt this and let us not compete amongst ourselves as to who is a greater Serb. See. That is what is what I said to him. Those who love the Serb people should be rational Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm just reading on: "Please, if we acquire the territories which we agree on and have conceived of today, plus the corridor we get up there, we will have done, this generation will have done so much for the Serbian people that this debt will be impossible to repay. What will happen in reality, we will leave that to time, but it will be easier to achieve this now, once we establish the Serbian army, which we could have done earlier."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. It was the establishment of the army that was our agenda. So a war was being waged without an army. So that's what I was trying to say. And before this, Mr. Kalinic says Kljujic and Jerko declared that the Muslims had already established the TO. That is to say that they already established a Muslim army. The item on the agenda was the establishment of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, of course, there is no connection between one sentence and the other where you say, Please, if we acquire the territories, and It will be easier to achieve this now once we establish the Serbian army? Those, Mr. Krajisnik, according to you, are utterly unlinked; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they are linked. We have a territory. If no one defends it and others attack it, we are not going to safeguard that territory. It says here that we are to defend the territory that is - how should I put this? - that is Serb. It was not established for us to attack. That's what I said. We are not taking what belongs to others. There is a sentence here stating that. We don't need the war option to take what belongs to others. I said here that we were in favour of the political option, not the war option, and that those who want to take the territory belonging to others are in favour of the war option. That's what I said here in the conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, not what belongs to others, Mr. Krajisnik, just Serbian ethnic territory, including those territories in which Serbs were a minority because of the genocide of World War II, right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This sentence, that's written here, that's what I said. That's what I said then. I said those who are in favour of the war option want to take what belongs to others. Whereas we just want our own. That's what it says here. If you want to discuss these other things, then I agree, but what I said is what is written here. If you want to, I will read it out to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Before the break, Mr. Krajisnik, I'm going to go back to our original discussion about the cease-fire, which as we saw from the Secretary-General's statement, was broken on June 26th during the course of operations around Dobrinja. And if I could ask -- well, first of all, those operations, Mr. Krajisnik, were offensive actions, weren't they? Those actions by the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Possibly. I don't know. Probably. I don't know. I don't know what these actions were like. Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's look at a document that indicates that in fact you did know, Mr. Krajisnik. That would be tab 167, Your Honour. Tab 167 are the minutes of the 12th session of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that is P64, P65, tab 171, Your Honour. At this session of the Presidency, Mr. Krajisnik, as you will see, present were Dr. Koljevic, Mrs. Plavsic, Dr. Djeric, and you.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we look at item 3 on this session that was held on June 27th --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 27th?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 27th.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We see that on this date, the Main Staff was ordered to cease all artillery and infantry operations in the suburb of Dobrinja, the order is given to dig in and move from offensive to defensive positions.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Then we said that all shelling should be stopped because Mr. Koljevic received this kind of information from MacKenzie and he insisted, as far as I can remember, or Mrs. Plavsic -- although, well, this meeting did not have the right to give orders, but it was sort of a warning to the Main Staff, because this was a complaint that came from Mr. MacKenzie. And that's what we did. Quite simply, we reacted. It doesn't have to mean that it was offensive. Only the information received said that it was offensive. Well, maybe it was offensive. I don't know. And what is written here is exactly what you said; that is to say, to move from defence to offence, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So the chronology is there was a cease-fire declared, it was broken in order to launch offensive operations against Dobrinja, to consolidate the Bosnian Serb hold in that area, there were complaints so significant that the Secretary-General went to the Security Council, and then the Presidency ordered, in response, that the army move from those offensive operations to defensive positions.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a consultative meeting. Mr. Koljevic had had a meeting with Mr. MacKenzie -- or was it Mrs. Plavsic? I don't know exactly. They conveyed what he had said about Dobrinja. And the recording clerk probably wrote down everything he said, and we said that this action had to be ended urgently, if that is what was concluded, and it was concluded this way. I don't even know who began, who started this, and I was not with MacKenzie, I was not on the spot. I don't know. But this was done just in case, because this was politically damaging to us, even if the Muslims had attacked us. This is what it says here, just fire if -- in cases of absolute necessity, because that is what was being said all the time. To this day, this is what soldiers are claiming, that they fired only when attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, I know the Court may have a question but I was watching the clock for the last five minutes. I didn't want to overextend the Court's indulgence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I had no question at this moment. We'll then have a break until five minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, it has been brought to our attention that you would like to refer to a publication from May, 1993, which you deem relevant in respect of the answer you've given on a Banja Luka television broadcast portion which was put to you by Mr. Tieger. I've asked to have this put on the ELMO so that we -- I hope we can read it. If you would please slowly read, starting just a little bit above the yellow highlighted portion, where we see that a portion is singled out. Can the interpreters see it on the screen? Would you please very slowly read it, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "After him, Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, spoke. 'I hope that we will lower tensions and play things down, because I see that there is bad blood between socialists and radicals,' said Raznjatovic, adding that 'Serbs don't need this.' He asked for a new agenda and for every MP to be given the right to speak, because otherwise, MPs nominated by citizens' groups would not have a voice, since they do not belong to any Deputies' Club. 'I'm sorry that the deputies from Republika Srpska did not come, probably because General Mladic forbade them, just as he forbade them in Bijeljina and threatened them against voting as they wished because they all declared themselves, as in old communist times, unanimously against the Vance-Owen Plan,' said Raznjatovic, and asked for a break with the practice of quarrelling and insults and also asking for somebody smart to come up and suggest an agenda."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that you wanted to draw our attention to this publication because it confirms what you said about that Arkan blamed Mladic for trying to keep people off from attending this Assembly. Is that well -- is that correctly understood, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I only made one mistake: It was on the 15th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. First of all we have now, I think, a better time frame for this television. At the same time, I think, but I might be wrong, that the issue raised by Mr. Tieger was not mainly on what was the reason why Arkan spoke and whether it had got something to do with Arkan blaming Mladic, but he mainly put the question to you, and I think that was the core of the issue, is where you in this television broadcast said something positive about Arkan, what positive you had in mind. I think that was the issue, and I did not, at least not at that moment -- at this moment, understand from Mr. Tieger's questions that he was disputing what had been said by Arkan, as far as blaming Mladic for keeping people off from -- so therefore, let's concentrate on the core of the issue, and this is not the core. The core was a different matter. Yes, okay. Let's proceed at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Mr. President, you have misunderstood this completely. My explanation, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I see is that you draw our attention at this moment to a document which supports what you told us about what the issue had been on which you commented at the time, and I -- you have an opportunity at the end of your testimony to add anything to that. Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I just ask what's going to happen to this newspaper article?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was about to -- it has been read at this moment. It seems to me not be of such vital importance. It's most importantly, I think, is that we have a time frame. Mr. Krajisnik said this was -- I said May, and whether it was 15 or 18, is to me not entirely clear, but that's also not, I would say, a vital issue. So therefore, this portion having been read and therefore being on the record, I would not insist at this moment on having it tendered into evidence. But if any of the parties would take a different view, of course, we'll then decide on admission into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, for that purpose it would be helpful to know the name of the publication and date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I ask that it be marked for identification at the moment, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, as a matter of fact, it seems very much to be Politika. Politika, and then whether it's 15th or the 18th of May is not entirely clear to me but it seems at least to be May, 1993, which -- no, it's the 15th of May. It appears from the cover page. It can be marked for identification. Mr. Registrar, that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D249 MFI, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, two quick additional matters before they escape my attention. First, the document referred to at the commencement of the session, 01245462, is not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then it needs a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P12 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's a document -- it's a D number, document produced by Mr. Krajisnik at the beginning of the session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D250, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- could someone remind me exactly on what it was? It was the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think I understood it to be a session of the government on July 29th, 1992, but I may be wrong about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Now I do remember. That is the -- yes, that's the -- yes. I've got it here. It is -- it's the cover page and the 9th page of the 43rd session of the government, 29th of July, 1992, and I think we were provided with a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There is a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of the whole of the document or just of the pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Of the whole of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it the whole of the document is there as well so that, if need be, we can look at it in a contextual way rather than just page 1 and page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The registrar now has electronically the whole of the document in English. He very helpfully provided me with a hard copy. And as Your Honour knows, well, the Defence have got the whole of the document in B/C/S, as of course do the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So then perhaps better admit the whole -- if it's nine pages, that's -- yes. Then Mr. Tieger, thank you for this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And one more quick matter in addition, Your Honour. If it wasn't -- the translations have been provided -- from yesterday, of those two newspaper articles, have been provided to the registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'd like to turn your attention next to a number of intercepts that you addressed during the course of your examination-in-chief on May 17th and May 18th of your testimony. Those are the intercepts involving Mr. Garic, and that will be found at tab 142, Mr. Karisik and Ninkovic, tab 141. And Mr. Milinkovic on -- that's found at -- been distributed, I think. I know you're already familiar with those because you discussed them at some length during your examination-in-chief. And those were intercepts -- at least the -- those were intercepts from April 21st, 1992. And in the course of discussing those intercepts and their significance, you were asked, for example, on the 17th of May, at page 45, beginning line 10: "Mr. Krajisnik, who is Mr. Garic?" You explained: "Mr. Garic is a man from Vraca, that is to say from Novo Sarajevo, whom I knew." Explained that he was an acquaintance. I think you said that Mr. Milenko Karisik was a policeman you knew, at page 47 of May 17th, at lines 5 and 6, and indicated that you couldn't recall Mr. Milinkovic's first name or face, but he was a "wonderful, very fine man." And that would be at page 61 of May 17th, at lines 1 through 4. And generally you explained that you wanted to know, on a personal basis, what was going on and so contacted people you knew from Sarajevo to satisfy your curiosity. And as stated, more specifically on page 47 on May 17th, at lines 15 through 16: "My communication with these people was on a personal basis." Now, I wanted, Mr. Krajisnik, to clarify some aspects of the conversations on that date. And perhaps we can begin with Mr. Garic, whom you said was a man you knew. In fact, Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Garic was a member of the Crisis Staff for Novo Sarajevo, I believe, and more specifically, he was the person as reflected in tabs -- excuse me, in additional items which I shall distribute now -- who was assigned certain significant positions within the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, those items are in evidence. The Crisis Staff meeting of December 23rd, 1991, is P529, tab 378. And the minutes of the Crisis Staff meeting held in Lukavica on January 29th, 1992, is P529, tab 260.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as we can see, Mr. Krajisnik, from the document of 23rd December, 1991, after -- during the course of assignments made following the discussion of materials received from the SDS BH main board, first degree. Mr. Garic, in item 9, was assigned Territorial Defence responsibilities, and as we can see in the -- from the record of the meeting on January 29th, 1992, item 10, he was assigned the task of ensuring that all battalion commanders be called to the Crisis Staff meeting. So Mr. Garic, Mr. Krajisnik, was not simply any neighbour of yours in Sarajevo; he was an SDS member, with some -- in fact a local leader with some significant responsibilities within the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know what position he held at that time. I was not aware of these assignments of his either.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when you called him on April 21st, 1992, you simply called him as a neighbour who might have some idea of what was going on rather than as an official who was involved with the operations of that day?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I called that number that I got, and I got him on the phone, and since I knew him, I asked him about what was going on there. Had somebody else been on the line, I would have asked him too, but then since he happened to be on the line, I talked to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, so you weren't calling Mr. Garic as a private personal matter, you were calling him for some specific reason, and he happened to be the person who was functioning in that capacity. What was that reason?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two telephone conversations here with Mr. Garic that were interrupted. I wanted to know what was going on in Vraca because there was an area I was interested in. Now, did I call him or did he call me? I think I was the one who called Vraca and then he answered the phone and I knew him and I asked what was going on there, and it was private, of course, because I knew the man. I cannot even remember what he looks like now but I knew him then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Karisik, he wasn't simply a personal acquaintance, he was a head of the RS special forces for the MUP, right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was commander of the special unit, the special Serb unit, when the special unit of the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina split up. And he was located in Vraca.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's take a look at what was going on that day, Mr. Krajisnik, to see how personal these calls were or how operational they were. First of all, if we could look at an item we'll distribute now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is P623.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's a conversation between Mr. Garic and Zoka in April, 1992. And as we can see from the first page, Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Garic says: "They don't want, you say. Who does not want?" Zoka: "Well, his, screw it, that is that ..." Garic: "They don't want, do they?!" Zoka: "This group that go with, with Brno." Garic: "They don't want, do they?!" Zoka: "Yes! He'll come with his eight." And then further on down, Garic: "No, he isn't. Well, do something, bring in the reinforcement over there ..." Zoka: "Who can in bring in, damn it?" Garic: "... Brne, as much as possible." Zoka: "But, whom can I bring in?" Garic: "I don't know. But, does anyone know who those 25 ... are, I mean, how many? 17 of them refused ..." And on the second page, we see that Mr. Garic wants to know what Tomo said in the meeting. And a couple of lines later, says: "Listen, you should see about it with Vojo, up there, Milinkovic. There are more of these men." And if we turn to tab 140, you'll see Mr. Garic again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This needs a number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1232, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Garic calling, wanting to know if it's Ilidza. Velibor says -- and I should indicate for the record that's an intercepted conversation on 21 April, 1992. The response is: "No, it isn't. It's the Serbian municipality of Ilidza, fuck it." Garic: "It's Momo. Is that Velibor?" Velibor: "It is." And then Garic goes on to say: "How can you assist us with manpower as soon as possible?" Velibor: "In manpower?" Garic: "Yeah." And Garic further on down the page: "They are coming from all sides. The army won't use tanks, nothing." Velibor: "They won't even move the tanks?" Garic: "No, no, no. By God, Velibor, do you have anything?" Velibor: "Come on, call Prstojevic, down there." And Garic, at the bottom, says: "If you make it, gather those fellows and send them to Vraca, please." So this is a reflection, Mr. Krajisnik, unless you have information to the contrary, that Mr. Garic is seeking reinforcements as aggressively as possible for an operation, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about this, but may I just draw your attention to this point where he says, "They are coming on from all sides. And the army won't move their tanks." That could mean that they were under attack. I don't know. I cannot comment. It's obvious that he's asking assistance from Ilidza, but this remark, "They are coming all from all sides," it sounds as if he's defending himself, whereas the army won't move. They won't move their tanks, they won't do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, look next at an intercept in which Mr. Garic in fact calls Mr. Prstojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That will need a number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1233 [Realtime transcript read in error "P1223"], Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The transcript has got the number wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1233, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Here, we see Garic asking first to speak to Danilo, and then he explains further on Veselinovic, and asking, "Is Prstojevic there?" and indicating he's calling from Novo Sarajevo. That's all on the first page. Then as we continue, the second page Garic wants to know from Prstojevic: "How can you help us as soon as possible?" And Prstojevic asks: "Yes, but where, what is your location?" Garic says: "In Vraca. We need some men in Vraca urgently, please." And after some specifics about that, Prstojevic asks: "Wait a second Garic, are you at the pass and further on up the right side, towards Vrace?" And Garic says: "We went down to the town all the way to the Miljacka river, but they're too strong there, they are encircling us and the army refuses to move." And he continues, about six lines down: "How can you help us? I also called Velibor in Nedzarici and he will try to do something, but that is not enough. That is not enough." Prstojevic: "All right. What are the Special Forces doing?" Garic: "They refuse to leave the barracks area. The Special Forces refuse to leave the barracks area. That's it. The reserve police force also promised to do everything they can but they went back." And finally, on the second-to-last page, in the middle, Prstojevic asks: "Where are you fighting exactly, where exactly are you ..." And Garic says: "Vrbanja, Grbavica, Ivan Krndelj, all the way to Elektroprivreda." So Mr. Krajisnik, I had those -- presented those intercepts to you so we could see the situation on April 21st, 1992, the date you had your conversations with Mr. Garic and others. And in that connection, I'd now like to turn to the intercepts you discussed in your testimony. If we could turn first to tab 141. We can see at the beginning this is a conversation -- this is P67, tab 30, Your Honour. Conversation on 21 April, 1992, with Mr. Ninkovic, Milenko Karisik, Mr. Krajisnik, and Nikola Koljevic. Now, the call is initiated by Branko who, as we can see about midway through the first page, is calling in order to put you on the phone. And he's -- and he states: "We are calling from the headquarters in Vraca." Then he goes on: "Hold on, please. Speaker Krajisnik is here." Now this is one of those calls that was made -- one of those personal calls, Mr. Krajisnik. Is it just coincidental that you happened to be in the headquarters in Vraca at the time you're making it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't at Vraca. Karisik was at Vraca. I was at Pale with Mr. Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, then the call must be being transferred through. In any event, Branko puts you on the phone and says, indicating that President Krajisnik is there.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mr. Branko says, "Here am I, calling from Pale." It's a mistake that I was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, that -- it's also not clear to me whether the phone -- whether the telephone conversation had been put through, because Branko -- yes, he says -- as a matter of fact, he says two different things.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Two opposite things. I don't even know who this Branko is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It could even be, Mr. Tieger, I don't know whether you have considered or whether it should be checked in the original, that the line starting with Branko, "We are calling from the HQ in Vraca, who am I talking to?" that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The answer is: "This is Branko here."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so that Branko is one line too far up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I hear Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That might be an explanation where Branko said earlier, "I'm calling from Pale" at the previous line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: M'hm. And I'll look at it again, but that certainly makes sense. And we have Mr. Krajisnik's testimony on where he was at the time the call was made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If there is any need to have it corrected, then we'll hear from you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. But I understood that I called from Pale, because Karisik was at Vraca, he wasn't at Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Then you indicate, it's Momo Krajisnik here. What's going on down there? And Ninkovic says, well, Karisik can explain better. It continues on the next page, with Karisik offering his explanation in response to your -- well, you tell him: "Tell me, what's the situation like down here -- down there? I hear there is chaos there." And Karisik said: "Well, there is lots of shooting down there. The members of the TO are engaged." That was a portion you discussed during the course of your examination-in-chief and that prompted some questions by the -- by His Honour the Presiding Judge. But further on down the page after Karisik says: "It's mainly members of the TO who are engaged ..." you say: "Yes, yes. It's chaos and the army can't engage because then we would have real problems. Can you make contact with them just so we know how they are doing? I need to know this, damn it." Now, Mr. Krajisnik, "I need to know this, damn it," from the president of the Assembly who has initiated a call in the middle of these kinds of -- this kind of operation, to the head of the Special Forces, doesn't sound like a personal call. Can you tell us what's personal about that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in Sarajevo, you received news that somebody launched some sort of adventurous operation and that there are casualties, and you are curious to know what is going on. So you call people you know to get more information. That's what it's all about. Doesn't matter that I'm speaker of the Assembly. I called Garic, Milinkovic. It's the 21st of April, just a few days after my arrival in Pale, which was on the 18th. Or maybe the 20th, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you actually spoke with Mr. Garic multiple times, or a number of times that day. If we look quickly at tab 143, another conversation of April 21st --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Koljevic is also involved in this conversation. He was expecting members of the European Union for a meeting. Maybe that's another reason why I called. Karisik was at a meeting. I don't remember this conversation, although it probably happened. I mean, I know that I called regarding that problem, whether I called him or somebody else, but it says Koljevic here. The representatives of the European Community were interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You testified about Dr. Koljevic's part of that conversation during the course of your examination-in-chief, but perhaps the nature of these phone calls can be made clearer if we look at other phone calls made on that same day. That's why I directed your attention to page -- to tab 143, which is a conversation between yourself and an unidentified male on 21 April, 1992. That's P625. And there, you ask is Momo Garic there and whether that's the Vraca Crisis Staff and are told this is the Vraca local community. You identify yourself and indicate that Garic just called you from somewhere and asked, "Is he with you? Do you know where he just called me from?" And you're provided with a number, and on the next page you say: "All right. Tell me, what's new? What's the situation like down there?" And are told: "Well, one part is withdrawing." You say: "Our men?" Answer: "Yeah." Your question: "Can they withdraw?" Answer: "Well, they've tried. They went down there to try to get those men out of encirclement." And we heard in an earlier intercept that was the nature -- at least, part of the nature of the problem that day. And then if we look at tab 142.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 142, you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, P67, tab 29, a conversation between you and Mr. Garic, someone calls on your behalf. This is a conversation you also looked at during the course of your examination-in-chief. And here you obviously reach Mr. Garic after the interruption and after the phone call in which you obtained his number in the previous exhibit, saying on the top of the second page: "Hey, Momo! Something interrupted us." And you say: "What is it? Tell me, what's the situation like?" Garic: "Well, there are some little problems. Can you receive me up there for a brief meeting?" You say: "Well, sure, no problem." And then further down: "All right, Momo. What's the situation up there?" Garic: "Well, it's all right for the time being. We've had some casualties and many wounded." You say: "You did? Well, are our men withdrawing from up there?" Garic: "No, no, but the cooperation here is not on a high level. I don't know why. They're ..." You say: "All right. Momo, come here, let's not discuss this over the phone." And finally, Mr. Krajisnik, if you'll turn to tab 144. That's P625, Your Honour. Conversation on -- again on April 21st between Mr. Prstojevic and an unknown male. Mr. Prstojevic identifies himself and asks: "Is Garic there?" And is told Garic went to Pale. And is asked to whom he's speaking and told by one of Garic's associates. Prstojevic: "All right. This is Prstojevic speaking, commander of Crisis Staff Ilidza." He indicates further down that he sent the help and manpower over there, that they continue talking about the situation. Then the unknown male says, about ten lines down from that: "Well, yes. But that's not very organised. The police doesn't want to come out and do their job. One part of the territory is already taken, but the police doesn't want to come out, so the people ... I don't know what to tell you, we have problems, there." Prstojevic: "Tell me how far will they go? Did you come to the left bank of the river Miljacka?" And the unknown male says: "Yes, this part is taken almost to the Miljacka river but the upper part, Ivan Krndelj Street, that is still not taken." Prstojevic: "And did you cut through Vrbanja?" And the male says: "Yes." Prstojevic: "And you are in control there?" And the male says: "Well, we are for the moment, but the police still didn't come out, so the civilians are holding that, fuck." Prstojevic: "Territorial Defence members?" And the unknown male says: "Well, yes." Prstojevic: "All right, but the police should come out." And the unknown male, Mr. Garic's associate, says: "Of course it should, but it's not and that's the problem. So Krajisnik called him and he went up there so they can agree on them doing their job, and if they don't want ... fuck it, they are not doing anything for the last 20 days." Now, Mr. Krajisnik, having now had an opportunity to look at the conversational exchanges that took place on that date, in which men were encirclement after having taken territory down to or almost down to the Miljacka, and the police weren't doing their job, and Garic calling you for -- to resolve that problem, isn't it the case that this was -- that your conversations on that date were anything but the curious inquiries of some neighbourhood busybody who was interested in what might be happening?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already responded, when I said that I was interested in what was going on there, but from these conversations I see that Garic first called me and then we got interrupted, we got disconnected, and then I called him back. And this end person, this unidentified person, says that Garic was asking to see me. He was asking to be received by me. And that was on a purely personal basis, a person who wanted to tell me what was going on. I wasn't calling Petrovac or Banja Luka. I was calling the area where I was living. That's certainly the long and short of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the fact is that in the middle of a battle which was -- in the middle of an operation, I should say, an offensive operation, in which things weren't going well, you made a series of phone calls to determine the status and Mr. Garic went to see you to resolve the critical problem which was that the police were not doing what he wanted them to do. That's the fact of these conversations --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You are completely, completely, you are completely wrong. Please, the operation was finished. It ended unsuccessfully at the point when I found out something, and I was trying to find out how many dead there were. And after it was all over, he was asking how to get people out. People were encircled and they needed to be pulled out. I heard about that tragedy, probably. Djeric, Koljevic and I, all of us who were up there were interested in finding out. You have the intercepts. You can see. How would I not be interested in what was going on there after hearing such news?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: My last question, because I know we are pressed: Mr. Krajisnik, these reflect your hands-on knowledge of operations in Sarajevo at the time they were happening. All of this was happening on April 21st. You were calling to find out what was happening and they were -- and the people most intimately involved in those operations, and most responsible for those operations, were advising you and coming to see you.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Prosecutor, you've read here that Garic first called me to tell me the news. Then we got disconnected. Then I called him back to ask what is going on. Then he asked can I come and see you? And he called Prstojevic and all the other men afterwards. I had nothing to do with it. Just I heard about the action, I heard about the unfortunate event, and all the people who got killed. If he did come later, he must have told me. I was interested in what is going on with those people who were encircled. You see that I had to ask who started that operation. If I had known, I wouldn't have had to ask who started that operation and got people killed, if there was anybody else involved there. It's all on -- in these papers. I don't know how you draw the conclusion that I was abreast of this operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I'm looking at the clock. We are far beyond the time already. But I still owe a response of the Chamber to your request, Mr. Josse. The Chamber has carefully listened to what you submitted. Mr. Josse, we have also carefully listened to Mr. Krajisnik's own submissions in this respect, and the Chamber has come to the conclusion that there is no reason not to sit tomorrow. So therefore, we'll sit tomorrow. There is another matter, but we might not be able to resolve. Mr. Krajisnik we learned that you have another appointment with the dentist next Wednesday. Is that again at 8.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. On Wednesday. 8.00. I just found out today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, we'll have to consider whether on that Wednesday, we could have a late start or whether we would swap for the afternoon but of course the first question will be whether the treatment you will undergo at that day allows at all for that day to sit. I've got no clue yet on what exactly the treatment is, but perhaps we, and you as well, or the Defence, might gain further information as to whether the treatment is such that it would prevent us from sitting that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I understand the Chamber to be saying that Mr. Krajisnik can definitely have the treatment that morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if it takes you a week to get an appointment, I mean, otherwise, we can't say until the end of the Defence case you cannot be treated by a dentist. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, we will further look on our agenda and see whether -- but as a matter of principle, if there is an appointment made with a specialist, especially when it's part of an ongoing treatment, which we do understand, so it has started already, we are inclined to agree with that. So we'll further look at how to deal with it, and of course if it would, for example, if we would -- if there would be a splendid solution to have the treatment done on Tuesday or Thursday without losing any day in court, then of course we would suggest, if possible, that the appointment with the dentist would perhaps then move to Tuesday or Thursday. So this is not a final yes but a yes in principle that everyone who needs treatment by a dentist will receive it in due time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: One other brief matter. Is the Chamber making any inquiry, either through one of its Legal Officers or through the Registry, as to the medication Mr. Krajisnik is presently taking or does the Chamber want the Defence to do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have not done that although we have taken some initiative to find out whether Mr. Krajisnik can have at his disposal I would say the ordinary painkillers which we all use now and then, like Aspirin, which in all our experience does not affect our normal daily ability. So we set out a request to be informed about that, but perhaps, Mr. Krajisnik, you could tell us, if you need an Asprin or something like that as a painkiller, are they available to you, in your experience?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I just explained what this was all about. The nerve was removed and then the canal is treated. I don't know what it is inside. So I just need to get this job done. Oh, I don't need Asprin, no, no. I have three different Asprins that I take, for allergy and all sorts of things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we'll further inquire into what actually -- what medication is taken, although Mr. Krajisnik seems not to be very worried about it and does not seem to indicate that at this moment it's something that he didn't used to take.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm just anxious to know if the Chamber are going to do this, because if they are not, the Defence will undertake some inquiries, but clearly we don't want to inundate the Detention Unit with requests --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please liaise with Mr. Zahar, perhaps tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll do that in the morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And then we will adjourn and with the apologies to the interpreters and the technicians for the very late finish today. And we will resume tomorrow afternoon at quarter past 2.00 in the same courtroom (sic).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 9th day of June, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 24

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.14 p.m.,
